name: Pennsylvania Dutch (Midwest)
family: Indo-European, Germanic, West Germanic, High German, Rhine Franconian (Palatine base)
variety: Pennsylvania Dutch (Pennsylvania German) of the Amish settlements of the American Midwest: Holmes County (Ohio), Elkhart and LaGrange counties (Indiana), Kalona (Iowa), Arthur (Illinois); text in the Buffington-Barba spelling
sources: Keiser, Steven Hartman (2012). Pennsylvania German in the American Midwest. Publication of the American Dialect Society 96. Durham: Duke University Press.
Keiser, Steven Hartman (2009). When 'speech islands' aren't islands: parallel independent development, drift, and minimal levels of contact for diffusion. Diachronica 26(1).
Louden, Mark L. (2016). Pennsylvania Dutch: The Story of an American Language. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.
Buffington, Albert F. and Barba, Preston A. (1954). A Pennsylvania German Grammar. Allentown: Schlechter's.
Van Ness, Silke (1994). Pennsylvania German. In König and van der Auwera (eds.), The Germanic Languages. London: Routledge.
Fasold, Ralph W. (1980). The conversational function of Pennsylvania Dutch intonation. Paper presented at NWAVE IX, Ann Arbor.
eSpeak NG voice and phoneme files for pdc-x-midwest (espeak-ng-data/lang/gmw/pdc-x-midwest, phsource/ph_pennsylvania_german_midwest), whose comments state the dialect features the voice assumes.
contrasts: short versus long vowels, with a difference of quality: /ɪ/ versus /iː/, /ɛ/ versus /eː/, /ʊ/ versus /uː/, /ʌ/ versus /oː/, /ɑ/ versus /ɔː/
the monophthong from ei, about [ɛː], is close to /eː/ and may be merging with it (Keiser 2012), so that pairs such as Deitsch and words with ee depend on a small difference of height
back rounded long /ɔː/ (written aa) versus /oː/ (written oo)
palatal and velar fricatives [ç x] and the weak voiced fricative [ɣ] between back vowels
allophony: ei is a long monophthong, about [ɛː] (Deitsch [dɛːtʃ], heit, Leit); it stays a diphthong [aɪ] before an unstressed vowel (Scheier, Feier); this monophthong is the main marker of Midwestern speech (Keiser 2009, 2012)
au is a long monophthong [aː] according to the voice files (Haus [haːs], Gaul [ɡaːl]); monophthongs for au are also reported for Amish speech in Illinois

/r/ is a tongue-tip tap after a consonant and between vowels and the American English approximant [ɹ] at the start of a word, according to the voice files; Keiser (2012) treats the variation between the older tap and the English-like approximant as a main consonantal variable of the Midwest
/r/ after a vowel is vocalised to [ɐ] or lost, giving centring diphthongs and a final [ɐ] for -er
/l/ is clear in all positions according to the voice files; Keiser (2012) studies the variation between clear and dark /l/
front vowels keep their height before a vocalised /r/ according to the voice files
some words differ in form from Pennsylvania: darich 'through' is deich and schtarick 'strong' is schteich according to the voice files
the lenis stops /b d ɡ/ are voiceless unaspirated lenes; the historical fortis /p t/ fell together with them in native words, while /k/ stays aspirated before a vowel
between vowels, historical /b/ is [v] and historical /ɡ/ is [j] after front vowels and [ɣ] after back vowels
ch is palatal [ç] after front vowels and consonants and velar [x] after back vowels
s is voiceless in all positions and is [ʃ] before p and t
obstruents are voiceless at the end of a word
unstressed e is schwa; unstressed -er is [ɐ]
English loans are frequent and are said with English sounds to a degree that depends on the speaker
phonotactics: onset clusters with /ʃ/ before p, t, m, n, l, r, w and with /ɡ/ or /k/ before n and l; prefix vowel loss gives clusters such as gsch- and gf-
final unstressed -n of German is lost
short stressed vowels are followed by a consonant, which the spelling doubles

stress.rule: Stress falls on the first syllable of the stem; the prefixes ge-, be-, ver- (fer-), er-, zer- are unstressed, separable particles and the first member of a compound are stressed, and loans keep the stress of the source word.
stress.cues: pitch movement, duration and intensity; unstressed syllables have schwa or [ɐ]

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: unstressed syllables mostly have [ə] or [ɐ]
rhythm.notes: No instrumental rhythm measurements are known to me.

length.notes: Vowel length is contrastive and tied to quality; the monophthongs from ei and au are long. Consonants are not long.

intonation.declarative: peaks on accented syllables, final fall to low
intonation.yes_no_question: rise to the last accented syllable followed by a fall on the syllables after it (a final rise-fall), as described for Pennsylvania; I know of no separate description for the Midwest
intonation.wh_question: accent on the question word, final fall
intonation.continuation: rise or high level at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: peak on the accented syllable followed by a fall
intonation.notes: Low confidence: the question pattern is documented for Pennsylvania (Fasold 1980) and carried over here.

problems: the stops b, d, g are inherited from the German table and are fully voiced; the descriptions have voiceless lenis stops

the monophthong from ei is a fixed [ɛː] (formant file vowel/e_8); the gradient, speaker-dependent range between diphthong and monophthong and its closeness to /eː/ that Keiser measured cannot be shown
yes-no questions use tune q4, which ends in a rise; the pattern documented for Pennsylvania Dutch is a rise to the accented syllable followed by a final fall
stress is put on the first syllable of words that carry it later (Babbier is [ˈbɑbiːɐ])
English loans that keep their English spelling are read by the German-type letter rules; the pronunciation list has about 260 entries
the pronunciations have not been checked by native speakers (the voice is marked 'testing')
good: ei is a monophthong except before an unstressed vowel (Deitsch [dɛːtʃ] but Feier [ˈfaɪɐ]), the condition Keiser reports

two Midwestern word forms are entered in the list: darich is said [dɛːç] and schtarick [ʃtɛːk] (the voice file names the forms deich and schteich, so the final [k] of the second entry does not match its own note)
r is a tap inside the word and an approximant word-initially; l is clear
the unrounded vowel system, vocalised r, intervocalic [j] and [ɣ] and final devoicing follow the descriptions

notes: Keiser's study rests on interviews in Kalona (Iowa) and Holmes County (Ohio), with comparison groups in Wisconsin and in Pennsylvania. His reviewers summarise that Pennsylvania speakers keep [aɪ] nearly without exception, apart from the position before /r/ and /l/, and that Midwestern speakers do not monophthongise before an unstressed vowel. The assignment of tap, approximant and clear l to positions follows the eSpeak NG voice files. No formant values are given because I cannot quote Keiser's measurements with confidence.
